title: Package Maintenance and Troubleshooting
subtopics: Finding which package owns a file
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of Package Maintenance and Troubleshooting and identify key concepts from the supplied syllabus.

content.intro: This lesson introduces package maintenance and troubleshooting as part of package management and software installation. Begin with an observation you can safely repeat, then explain what the result tells you and what it does not prove.
content.why_it_matters: Choose distribution-appropriate package tools, reason about trusted repositories, and plan updates or rollback.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Package managers track software and dependencies from configured sources. Trust the repository, review changes, and plan maintenance windows.

items.title: Broken dependencies
items.text: Broken dependencies: Identify the concept’s role in the workflow, choose a read-only inspection first, and record the version or distribution details that could change the result.

content_blocks.run_instructions: Use a Linux machine, WSL environment, or disposable virtual machine. Check the command with its local manual page before adapting it. The in-page example shows reference output only; it does not execute Bash/Linux commands on the CodeLeaf server. Commands and output formats may vary by distribution and installed utility version.
content_blocks.reset_steps: These example commands are read-only or print-only. Exit the terminal when finished; if you adapt the task to create files, use a disposable practice folder and remove only the test files you deliberately created.
content_blocks.example_review_note: Topic-specific draft example authored for Linux course. Output is environment-dependent where stated; review on the target distribution before publishing.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: First, state what you expect from the example. Run it in the intended environment, capture standard output and any error message, and inspect the exit status where meaningful. Then connect the observation to this lesson: Package Maintenance and Troubleshooting. Do not infer more than the evidence supports.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake
content_blocks.text: A common mistake is to assume package maintenance and troubleshooting behaves identically on every distribution, kernel, utility version, and administrative policy. Verify the installed tool and consult the matching manual before using the procedure elsewhere.

content_blocks.title: Safety and compatibility
content_blocks.text: Planning output only; do not partition or install on a machine with important data for this exercise. For commands that edit files, manage services, change network/firewall state, partition disks, change permissions recursively, or alter boot settings, use an isolated VM, take a snapshot/backup, review the exact target, and prepare a recovery path before acting.

content_blocks.title: Troubleshooting and reset
content_blocks.text: If the command is missing, check whether the required package is installed and which distribution you are using. If access is denied, do not immediately escalate to root; confirm the target path, identity, and required permission. If the result differs, capture the command, output, version, and environment so the issue can be reproduced.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: Remember the core relationship: Package managers track software and dependencies from configured sources. Trust the repository, review changes, and plan maintenance windows. The goal is to explain the observed result, test a boundary case, and record a limitation rather than memorize a command in isolation.

content.task: In an isolated Linux lab, investigate package maintenance and troubleshooting. Use the guided example as a starting point, record the output/status, and test one boundary, failure, or distribution-specific case. Explain what you learned without changing a production system.
task_acceptance_criteria: The practical step is aligned to this lesson and uses synthetic inputs or a disposable environment.
The submission records expected and observed behavior, including an exit status or error when relevant.
One boundary case, failure path, or version/distribution difference is tested and explained.
Any potentially destructive command is previewed and kept out of production; the result can be reproduced.
hints: Start with read-only inspection and use the manual page for the installed command.
Change one variable at a time and preserve the exact output/error.
Record the distribution, kernel/utility version, privileges, and any assumptions that affect the result.
recap: Package managers track software and dependencies from configured sources. Trust the repository, review changes, and plan maintenance windows.
Use evidence rather than assumptions; make platform differences explicit.
Protect credentials and data, and plan how to reverse state-changing operations.
